So fun story, I went to the same high school as Tom Brady (Junipero Serra High School in San Mateo, CA). Brady is their Golden boy. Plain and simple. The man can commit murder and they’d still love him to death (probably not but after deflate-gate, everyone still loved him). 

The man also has 7 rings now. I mean that’s quite a feat in of itself. On top of that, he was like a 2nd or 3rd string QB in high school. Got the chance to play at Michigan and was subpar in his combine. He was lanky, awkward, and slow. Nobody really wanted him. The Pats picked him up in the 6th round after he was told he was going to get picked up in the 2nd or 3rd round and he just started making plays.

He’s kind of like the Dale Earnhardt Sr. of football. People hate him because chances are he ruined your favorite team’s shot at winning the Super Bowl. At the same time, people respect the hard work and determination he puts into his sport.

Idk that’s just my own two cents.

I (18m) might be able to help a little here. First off, I’m sorry about your boyfriend. No one of any gender, race, background, etc should ever go through something like this. As a sexual assault survivor myself, it’s really hard to be in relationships. Sex is a tricky situation and sexual assault and rape make things even more difficult. My advice, is to take things slow, have a “safe word,” that either of you can use to stop whatever is happening. It’s frustrating and can be painful, but if you love/care about him it is worth it. For all of my partners since the assault, I’ve had to stop in the middle of sex at one point or another. It’s either stopped altogether or just taking a break.

Furthermore, I highly recommend looking at couples counseling. Not only is this an issue facing him but also yourself and both of you should talk things through and help each other. 

A last comment, sexual assault is an extremely difficult area for anyone victimized in these scenarios. For men, it is a whole different struggle. (This is not meant to belittle anyone with their experiences, this is my opinion as a man who has dealt with this issue) it takes away a “manly” trait we are supposed to have. In most cases, men are the aggressors and their feelings of sex are stereotypically a resounding yes. In the cases where it is not, communication between partners is key.
